Immune cell population readout

Does miraclib response show up in the blood?

Relative frequencies of five immune cell populations across every sample in the trial, and the test of whether those frequencies separate melanoma patients who respond to miraclib from those who don't. Short answer: not by a margin that survives correction.

Part 2

Frequency of each population in each sample

Each sample's five counts are summed to a total, and each population is expressed as a percentage of that total. Filter to any project, condition or sample type — the table and the averages below recompute.

Part 3

Responders versus non-responders

Melanoma patients on miraclib, PBMC samples only. Each patient contributes up to three visits, so the same comparison is offered per sample and per subject — averaging a patient's visits first removes the pseudo-replication.

Populationn resp.n non-resp. Mean resp.Mean non-resp.Difference Rank-biserialpq (BH)Verdict

Two-sided Mann–Whitney U per population; Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control across the five tests at α = 0.05. Difference is in percentage points (responder minus non-responder). Rank-biserial is the effect size: +1 means responders are always higher, −1 always lower.

Part 4

The baseline cohort

Melanoma PBMC samples drawn on day 0 from miraclib-treated patients — the subset a predictive marker would have to work on, since it is all that exists before the drug is given. Exactly one baseline sample per subject, so sample and subject counts coincide.

How to read this, and what it can't tell you

The percentages are compositional: the five populations sum to 100% within every sample, so they cannot all move in the same direction. A rise in CD4+ T cells is necessarily a fall somewhere else, and the tests below treat each population separately rather than modelling that constraint.

The Mann–Whitney test is rank-based, which is the right choice here — the percentages are bounded at 0 and 100 and mildly skewed, so a t-test's normality assumption is not free. Five populations are tested at once, so raw p-values are corrected for the false discovery rate; the corrected value is the one to quote.

What this analysis is not: a model. It compares one population at a time and ignores covariates (age, sex, project) and the repeated-measures structure beyond the per-subject averaging offered above. A confirmatory analysis would be a mixed-effects model on log-ratio-transformed frequencies with subject as a random effect.
